Türkiye braces for sweltering August heatwave
ISTANBUL
Türkiye is set to experience a spell of intense summer heat in the first week of August, with temperatures expected to exceed seasonal averages across much of the country.
The hottest conditions are forecast for the southeastern provinces, where temperatures are likely to surpass 40 degrees Celsius, while high humidity is expected to make conditions particularly oppressive in Istanbul and other coastal parts of the Marmara region.
Climate scientist and meteorological engineer Hüseyin Toros of Istanbul Technical University said the period popularly known as eyyam-ı bahur — a traditional term referring to the hottest days of summer — is not an official meteorological phenomenon with fixed dates. While commonly associated with the period between late July and early August, its timing and intensity vary from year to year.
Current atmospheric forecast models indicate that temperatures will rise above seasonal norms across large parts of Türkiye from the middle of the week. According to Toros, the heatwave will be driven by hot air masses arriving from the Arabian Peninsula in the east and North Africa in the west, producing different impacts across the country.
The primary concern in southeastern Türkiye will be extreme air temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius, while residents of Istanbul are expected to face heightened discomfort due to elevated humidity levels, which will push perceived temperatures significantly higher.
Toros said long-term observations reveal a clear warming trend across Türkiye. Data from the Turkish State Meteorological Service show the country’s average annual temperature increased from 12.7 degrees Celsius during 1970-1980 to 14.4 degrees Celsius over the 2014-2025 period. The warmest year on record was 2024, with an average temperature of 15.3 degrees Celsius, while 1992 was the coldest at 11.4 degrees Celsius.
He warned that climate assessments indicate Türkiye is facing increasing risks from rising temperatures and more frequent extreme weather events. Future heatwaves are expected to become more common, longer-lasting and more intense, posing challenges for public health, water resources, agriculture, urban infrastructure and energy systems.
Toros also highlighted the urban heat island effect, where concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it overnight, keeping cities significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas. He called for expanding green spaces, increasing shaded areas and adopting urban planning measures that reduce heat accumulation.
Experts recommend avoiding prolonged outdoor activity between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., staying well hydrated, wearing light, breathable clothing, limiting direct sun exposure and scheduling physical activity during the early morning or evening hours.

Some work in temperatures exceeding 50 degrees Celsius
A worker looks over a construction site in Jung District, Seoul, Sunday. Korea Times photo by Na Min-seo
When a heat warning was issued across Seoul on Sunday, 50-year-old Lee stood gasping for air at a construction site in central Seoul. His attempt to cover his arms and neck with sun-protective sleeves proved futile against the scorching heat, and his work clothes were drenched in sweat.
“It’s literally raining sweat here,” Lee said. “I’m soaked through to my underwear. But I’m dreading next week, which they say is going to be even worse.”
Temperatures in Seoul peaked at 35 degrees Celsius that day. For construction workers surrounded by sun-baked concrete walls and steel frames, conditions were even more unbearable. A thermometer placed on an exterior wall read 39 degrees.
A thermometer at the construction site in Jung District, Seoul, reads 35 degrees Celsius. Korea Times photo by Na Min-seo
Nearby construction sites in central Seoul offered similar scenes. Exhausted workers sat in the shade with bottles of ice water in their hands, but even those did little to fend off the heat.
“We take a 10-minute break every hour, but there isn’t even a fan here, so all we can do is sit in the shade,” said Kim, 41. “I sweat so much that my clothes rub my skin raw wherever they touch.”
But workers say asking for sufficient breaks is not an option when they are working under tight deadlines.
“If you say you’re feeling unwell and need a break, what you’ll probably hear is, ‘You don’t have to come back tomorrow,’” said a construction worker at a site in Gwacheon. “That’s why everyone just keeps their head down and works.”
Downtown Seoul appears trapped beneath a heat dome in this thermal image taken from the 63 Building in Yeouido, Sunday, as a heat wave grips the country. Warmer areas appear redder in the image. Korea Times photo by Jang Ryeon-sung
Delivery workers also face growing risk of heat-related illness
Workers who spend much of their time on the road are also suffering in the heat. On the same day, Yoon, a 40-year-old parcel delivery driver, repeatedly wiped the sweat from his forehead as he unloaded some 200 packages from his delivery vehicle at an apartment complex in Seoul’s Mapo District.
“In summer, the temperature inside the cargo area easily exceeds 50 degrees Celsius. Just loading and unloading packages is an ordeal even before the actual deliveries begin,” he said.
“But I can’t stop working. Failing to meet the required quota results in a penalty, while taking a day off means a cut in pay.”
Similarily, food delivery riders ride across scorching asphalt while taking the heat. For them, summer is the most important yet dicey part of the year, because delivery orders surge in hot weather, but so do the risks of accidents and heat-related illness.
Delivery rider Cho Jung-hee prepares to drive off after loading packages in Dongjak District, Seoul, Sunday. Korea Times photo by Kwon Jung-hyeon
Shin, a 33-year-old delivery rider in Seoul’s Seodaemun District, had covered nearly his entire body with sun-protective clothing and fitted a sunshade over his motorcycle. But his eyes and the bridge of his nose, the only parts of his body left exposed, were beaded with sweat.
Shin said the only break he could manage was to take off his helmet and sip an iced coffee that had long since melted.
“It is suffocating to feel heat rising from the engine beneath me as I wait for the light to turn green,” he said.
Delivery riders receive an additional 500 won per delivery in weather like this, but the extra pay is not worth risking their lives for, Shin said.
As with construction workers, chafing caused by sitting on a motorcycle for hours in sweat-soaked clothes is one of the biggest difficulties delivery riders face. Lee Sae, 39, who makes deliveries in northern Seoul, said slathering protective skin care products over his body before leaving for work has become part of his daily routine.
Kim Yo-el, another rider working in Gyeonggi Province, said he occasionally feels the world spinning when he gets off his motorcycle during the day.
“But all I can do is find some shade and rest briefly by the roadside or on my motorcycle,” he said.
Calls grow to guarantee workers’ right to rest
Equally suffering from the heat are indoor parking lot staff, who have to endure the heat from car engines and sauna-like thick warm air.
"Internal feels-like temperature goes as far as 50 degrees celsius. Lacking ventilitation makes the experience feel like being inside a sauna," said Lee, 55, who manages the parking lot and collects shopping carts at a large supermarket in Gwangmyeong, Gyeonggi Province. He said he works eight hours a day in the parking lot, walking as many as 30,000 steps each day.
A parking attendant pushes shopping carts through the parking lot of Costco’s Gwangmyeong branch in Gwangmyeong, Gyeonggi Province, Sunday, as daytime temperatures reached 35 degrees Celsius.
Experts agree that measures to protect these workers are urgently needed.
“Day laborers at construction sites have no choice but to endure the heat because they fear they will be fired the moment they say it is too hot to work,” said Park Se-jung, head of occupational safety and health at the Korean Construction Workers’ Union. “The right to take breaks must be guaranteed by law so that workers can rest without worrying about losing wages.”
Song Ki-sun, head of the Nationwide Delivery Riders Association, also echoed a stronger safety measures for riders.
“There are rest shelters operated by local governments, but they are often difficult to access because they are located far from areas with high delivery demand or inside subway stations,” he said. “What riders need are rest areas along their delivery routes, even if they are small.”

The relentless heat, which shattered South Korea’s all-time temperature record in the southeastern city of Yangsan on Sunday, is showing no sign of easing, with the worst of it shifting toward the western and central parts of the country.
As of 1 p.m. Monday, severe heat wave warnings — the highest alert level that calls for an immediate halt of outdoor work — were in effect for the Gyeongsang region and parts of South Jeolla Province, while heat wave warnings were issued for most of the rest of the country.
Although lower than Sunday’s all-time national high of 42.5 degrees Celsius, temperatures remained extreme on Monday, with Daegu reaching 40.9 C, according to the Korea Meteorological Administration. Gwangyang in South Jeolla Province recorded a high of 40.3 C, while Yangsan, where the record was set a day earlier, reached 39 C. Seoul recorded 37.2 C.
With most regions forecast to continue to sizzle under the ongoing heat wave, central and provincial governments are operating in emergency mode to mitigate the impact.
Tropical nights
As of Monday morning, Seoul recorded 12 consecutive tropical nights in a row, while northern Jeju extended its streak to 27 nights, the longest currently recorded nationwide. Busan’s overnight temperature fell no lower than 28.5 C, while Yangsan remained at 28 C. Along the east coast, overnight lows stood at 26.7 C in Gangneung, 26.6 C in Donghae and 26.5 C in Sokcho.
Gangneung, Yangyang and Sokcho have now experienced tropical nights for seven consecutive days. The streak has continued for five days in Donghae, Samcheok and Goseong.

Government figures released Monday showed that 96 patients with heat-related illnesses were reported on Aug. 1 alone, bringing the cumulative total since May 15 to 1,889, including 14 possible heat-related deaths.
The death toll is expected to rise, as additional suspected heat-related deaths were reported Sunday in Busan and other areas.
In Dangjin, South Chungcheong Province, two elderly farmers were found collapsed after going out to work in the fields in separate incidents Sunday afternoon. The deaths, along with other possible cases, have not yet been officially confirmed as heat related.

Di Kyu-seok Shim, Daewoung Kim e Dahyun Lee
SEUL, 3 agosto (Reuters) - Un’ondata di caldo record sta attanagliando la penisola coreana, facendo impennare le temperature in tutta la Corea del Sud e nella Corea del Nord, mentre le autorità intensificano le misure di emergenza e i residenti cercano sollievo nei centri di raffreddamento, sulle spiagge e nei parchi acquatici.
Lunedì i meteorologi hanno affermato che il caldo estremo, precedentemente concentrato nel sud-est della Corea del Sud, si sta estendendo all’area metropolitana di Seul e ad altre regioni occidentali. Anche i media statali nordcoreani hanno segnalato temperature che sfiorano i 40 gradi Celsius (104 gradi Fahrenheit) in alcune zone del Paese e una quinta notte tropicale consecutiva a Pyongyang.
L’agenzia meteorologica sudcoreana ha avvertito che questa settimana le temperature potrebbero aumentare ulteriormente nelle regioni occidentali e ha affermato che l’ondata di caldo e le notti tropicali potrebbero persistere.
I dati diffusi domenica dall’Agenzia coreana per il controllo e la prevenzione delle malattie hanno mostrato che, da metà maggio, 14 persone sono morte e 1.889 hanno sofferto di disturbi legati al caldo.
L’Amministrazione Meteorologica Coreana (KMA) ha dichiarato che domenica a Yangsan sono stati registrati 42,5 °C, la temperatura più alta mai rilevata in 122 anni di osservazioni meteorologiche. La città, situata nel sud-est del Paese, aveva già battuto il record nazionale nei due giorni precedenti.
Il primo ministro Han Seong-sook ha ordinato ai ministeri e alle amministrazioni locali di mobilitare tutte le risorse disponibili per far fronte ai rischi legati all’ondata di caldo e alla siccità, dopo che il governo ha innalzato l’allerta per l’ondata di caldo al secondo livello più alto, sbloccando fondi per gli interventi di soccorso e ispezioni più frequenti nelle aree colpite.
Le autorità energetiche hanno attivato misure di emergenza e stanno monitorando attentamente l’offerta e la domanda, poiché si prevede che il consumo di elettricità raggiunga un livello record alla fine di agosto a causa del forte aumento dell’uso dei condizionatori.
Lunedì l’Agenzia meteorologica coreana (KMA) ha emesso il suo primo avvertimento in assoluto di ondata di calore grave per alcune zone di Seul e della vicina provincia di Gyeonggi, mentre gli stessi allarmi di calore di massimo livello sono rimasti in vigore in tutte le regioni meridionali, tra cui Busan, Ulsan, Gyeongsang del Sud e alcune zone di Gwangju e della provincia di Jeolla del Sud.
PARTITE DI BASEBALL ANNULLATE
Le amministrazioni locali si sono mobilitate per proteggere i residenti più vulnerabili. I distretti di Seul hanno ampliato i centri di refrigerio e distribuito gratuitamente acqua e ombrelli da sole, mentre Yangsan ha intensificato le operazioni di nebulizzazione d’acqua e la distribuzione idrica.
Le temperature torride hanno sconvolto la vita quotidiana. Durante il fine settimana, la Korea Baseball Organization ha annullato le partite a Busan e Changwon e ha dichiarato che potrebbero essere presi in considerazione ulteriori adeguamenti del calendario se le condizioni di pericolo dovessero persistere.
I media locali hanno riportato immagini di spiagge, parchi acquatici e aree ricreative lungo i fiumi affollatissime.
Lungo il torrente Cheonggyecheon di Seul, dove la città sta organizzando un festival estivo dell’acqua con zone temporanee per sguazzare e aree dedicate agli spruzzi, le famiglie hanno cercato sollievo dal caldo.
«Quaranta gradi non è una temperatura a cui eravamo abituati in Corea, ma ora sembra che la vediamo continuamente», ha affermato Park Jin-woo, 39 anni, che ha portato lì i propri figli per rinfrescarsi.
Lee Jub-young, 43 anni, residente a Seul, ha affermato che il caldo ha reso gli ombrelloni una necessità piuttosto che un accessorio di moda.
«Questa crisi climatica è diventata qualcosa che i cittadini possono sentire sulla propria pelle», ha detto.
La Corea del Nord sta vivendo condizioni simili. I media statali hanno riferito che gli avvisi di caldo che interessano gran parte del paese rimarranno in vigore per tutta la settimana e hanno segnalato che nel mese di luglio decine di migliaia di persone hanno visitato la zona turistica costiera di Wonsan Kalma.
Anche i parchi acquatici di Pyongyang erano affollatissimi, secondo la televisione di Stato.

'Like a giant boiling cauldron': How Korea's hottest city is coping with unbearable heat wave
Listen
By Hankookilbo
Published KST
Yangsan's commercial activity suffers as city hits nation's highest temperature ever
A vendor drinks cold water at Yangsan Nambu Market in Yangsan, South Gyeongsang Province, when the city's daytime high reached 42.5 degrees Celsius, Sunday. Yonhap
YANGSAN, South Gyeongsang Province — The streets of Yangsan, where Korea recorded its highest temperature ever at 42.5 degrees Celsius on Sunday, were nearly deserted except for delivery riders rushing between orders.
Outside a restaurant in Jungbu-dong, a delivery rider in his 40s repeatedly shifted his feet while waiting to pick up food, unable to bear the heat radiating from the sun-scorched asphalt. As the heat wave drove a surge in food delivery orders, he was fully equipped with cooling arm sleeves, a cooling vest and a neck cooler, but sweat still poured down his face.
Removing his helmet to wipe away sweat, he said, "It's so hot that I can't even stand still outside. The whole city feels like a giant boiling cauldron."
A vendor drinks iced water at Yangsan Nambu Market in Yangsan, South Gyeongsang Province, when the city's daytime high reached 42.5 degrees Celsius, Sunday. Yonhap
Yangsan has been gripped by an unprecedented heat wave after shattering the nation's all-time temperature record.
The city has been under the highest-level heat wave warning for nine consecutive days since July 25. Temperatures have exceeded 40 C for five straight days since Wednesday, peaking at 42.5 C at 1:26 p.m. Sunday, the highest temperature ever officially recorded in Korea.
The normally bustling Yangsan Youth Street and the Mulgeum New Town area were eerily quiet. The city appeared almost frozen by the extreme heat, with few pedestrians even during lunchtime. Those who ventured outside hurried along while covering themselves from head to toe with parasols, hats, sunglasses and cooling sleeves.
Unmanned ice cream shops and claw machine arcades became makeshift refuges where residents briefly escaped the heat.
"I only stepped out of my house for a moment, but I'm already drenched in sweat," one resident said. "Whenever I see an unmanned shop, I stop by because I can enjoy the air conditioning without worrying about bothering anyone."
The Yangsan Nambu Market in Yangsan, South Gyeongsang Province, is deserted on Sunday, the day when the temperature reached 42.5 degrees Celsius, marking the highest temperature ever officially recorded in Korea. Korea Times photo by Park Eun-kyung
Outdoor traditional markets were hit especially hard.
At Nambu Market, the city's commercial hub, customer traffic all but disappeared. Cooling fog systems installed every 5 meters continuously sprayed fine mist, but they offered little relief against temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius.
A vegetable vendor sighed while sorting through wilted produce.
"I picked this lettuce fresh from the field this morning, but after just a few hours, it's already gone limp and I can't even sell it," the merchant said.
Street vendors without proper fans faced even harsher conditions, enduring the blazing sun with little protection.
"When it gets too hot, I go into the Hanaro Mart inside the market for a while to cool down before coming back," said a street vendor in his 70s with an embarrassed smile.
Valley resort also suffers as drought empties streams
Popular outdoor recreation areas also looked very different from previous summers.
Hwangsan Park, which features camping facilities and water attractions and is usually packed with families on summer weekends, was relatively quiet. Most parking spaces were empty, and few people could be seen walking along its trails.
"Summer and winter are usually our off-seasons because we're a campground, but our water park normally pushes summer reservations to about 50 percent," a park official said. "This year they're only around 30 to 40 percent. I think people simply don't want to go outside because it's too hot."
Hwangsan Park Campground in Yangsan, South Gyeongsang Province, is sparsely occupied on Sunday, when the daytime high soared to 42.5 degrees Celsius. Korea Times photo by Park Eun-kyung
The situation was no better at Baenaegol Valley in Wondong-myeon, one of Yangsan's best-known summer destinations.
Although it was peak vacation season, restaurants and wooden platforms along the valley were largely empty. A severe drought left the streambed exposed after the region received only 40.7 millimeters of cumulative rainfall last month.
The prolonged drought, combined with the scorching heat, prompted Yangsan officials and local residents to hold a traditional rain prayer ceremony on Thursday, but rain has yet to arrive.
Kwon Ju-hee, 46, who visited from Busan with her family, expressed disappointment.
Wooden platforms outside a restaurant along Baenaegol Valley in Wondong-myeon, Yangsan, South Gyeongsang Province, sit empty at lunchtime on Sunday as the extreme heat keeps vacationers away. Korea Times photo by Park Eun-kyung
"We came to a nearby valley because we thought the beach would be too hot, but there's hardly any water here," she said. "Even where water has pooled, it's only knee-deep for an adult, and it's lukewarm, so soaking your feet doesn't help cool you down."
Son Hyun-sook, 54, who has operated a pension and grocery store in Baenaegol for 35 years, said the drought has become a serious threat to local businesses.
"Even though this is supposed to be a summer resort, we're facing water shortages and even restricted water supply," she said. "We depend on the summer season to make a living, but we're getting almost no reservation inquiries during what should be our busiest period. Now I'm worried about covering operating costs."
A water truck sprays the road in Nambu-dong, Yangsan, South Gyeongsang Province, Friday. Yonahp
City steps up emergency response
As heat-related challenges continue, Yangsan City has expanded its emergency response measures.
The city has allocated 144 million won (about $104,000) from its disaster management fund to increase the number of water-spraying trucks from five to 11 and extend their operation through early next month. The men died while working outdoors on Sunday as the heat pushed north and west.
The heatwave is now spreading towards Seoul, where temperatures are forecast to reach 38C.
A man in his 80s was found collapsed inside a greenhouse in Gimpo, a city just west of Seoul, at around 5pm local time, and was dead when emergency crews arrived, local authorities said. Another man died in similar circumstances in the southern port city of Busan.
Police believe both deaths were caused by heat but are still investigating.
The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency recorded about 1,900 cases of heat-related illness between mid-May and Sunday. That is below the roughly 2,800 cases logged over the same period last year, though officials expect the number to climb while temperatures remain high.
Rural areas accounted for over half the deaths recorded until late July, with many patients falling ill while working in greenhouses, rice paddies and fields.
The heat is now moving into the more heavily populated west, where about half of South Korea’s 51 million people live in and around the capital. Seoul was forecast to reach 37C on Monday, more than two degrees above Sunday's high, with some areas of the wider metropolitan area exceeding 38C, after easterly winds crossed the Taebaek mountain range and warmed as they descended on the western side.
The worst of the heat so far has been concentrated in the southeast. Yangsan, a city of about 350,000 in South Gyeongsang province, reached 42.5C at 1.26pm on Sunday, the highest temperature measured in South Korea since records began over a century ago, according to the Korea Meteorological Administration. Britain's own record, set at Coningsby in Lincolnshire in July 2022, is 40.3C.
Yangsan had broken the national record on Saturday at 41.6C before surpassing it again the next later, and went on to exceed 40C for five consecutive days. The city sits in a mountain basin that traps warm air and limits circulation, which forecasters say has amplified the heat there.
The heat extends across the border into North Korea. The news agency KCNA said that Pyongyang and the northern provinces of Phyongan and Jagang were forecast to experience daytime highs of between 35C and 40C.
Temperatures in the capital had not fallen below 25C at night since last Monday. Rodong Sinmun, the newspaper of the ruling Workers' Party, told people to avoid going outside during the day and issued advice to farmers about shielding crops from the heat and humidity.
In South Korea, the weather agency issued its highest level of extreme heat warning for eastern Gwangju as well as for the cities of Boseong, Yeosu, Gwangyang, Suncheon and Gokseong in the province of South Jeolla in the southwest.
The alert, introduced this year, is triggered when an area is forecast to reach an actual temperature of 39C or a perceived temperature of 38C for a day. More than 20 localities were under such warning on Sunday.

Prime minister Han Seong Sook ordered the use of all available resources to mitigate the impacts of the heatwave and the drought as the government raised the heatwave alert to the second-highest level and released funds for relief work.
Power authorities have begun emergency monitoring of supply and demand. Electricity use is expected to hit a record in late August as air conditioning runs harder.

Reservoirs across South Gyeongsang are down to 40 per cent of capacity, with at least two, both in the city of Miryang, close to empty and no longer able to supply water to farms.
Forecasters said scattered showers on Tuesday could ease the heat in southern areas, though highs of about 37C were still expected and humidity could push the heat index higher after the rain.
Extreme heat has gripped nearly all of East Asia. Japan recorded its first "cruelly hot day" last month after temperatures climbed past 40C in three cities, weeks after the weather agency introduced the term to warn people about dangerous heat.
The designation of cruelly hot day, “kokushobi” in Japanese, was coined in April for any day recording a temperature of 40C.

The Met Office predicts temperatures could soar to 35C in the South East on Monday, surpassing the expected highs for islands such as Mykonos, Rhodes, and Santorini.
Much of central and southern England is anticipated to experience highs in the upper 20s to low 30s before a slight easing later in the week.
In response, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued amber heat-health alerts for the East Midlands, East of England, South East, and London, effective from Monday until Wednesday morning.
This alert warns that the intense heat could place additional strain on the NHS, with vulnerable individuals more likely to require medical attention. Yellow heat-health alerts will also be in place for the North West, Yorkshire and The Humber, West Midlands, and South West during the same period.
Met Office forecaster Marco Petagna stated: "We’re going with a headline tomorrow of 34C, but with a potential for local 35C in the South East, the Midlands into the low 30s as well.

Tomorrow is the peak of the heat; temperatures do come down a little bit, we’re still talking 28 to 30C on Tuesday. Again, the South East and East Anglia we’re seeing the highest temperatures on Tuesday, so not as extreme as tomorrow, but still well above average."
He added: "And then even by Wednesday, we’re looking at high 20s, 26 or 27C, in the South East. But it’s a gradual cooling down process through the week, and always cooler towards the North and West in any case, high teens, low 20s, but certainly central and South East England seeing hot weather returning briefly, and a lot of sunshine to come in the South East as well."
Mr Petagna also noted that low pressure moving in from the west could bring rain to northern and western parts of the UK, with a chance of showers reaching the South East on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Simple steps such as staying hydrated, avoiding the sun during the hottest part of the day, and keeping your home cool are some of the key ways to help keep yourself and others safe during periods of hot weather."
Angelo Makri of the Alzheimer’s Society highlighted specific concerns for those with dementia: "People should absolutely enjoy the warmer weather, but it’s important to remember that high temperatures can pose serious risks for people living with dementia if they are not supported to stay cool and hydrated. People with dementia may not always recognise when they need a drink or wear suitable clothing, which can increase the risk of dehydration and heat-related illness. With temperatures set to reach extreme highs this week, we’re urging families, friends and carers to make sure loved ones are drinking enough, wearing light clothing and staying indoors as much as possible."

Nuclear plant shutdown looms as Hungary battles drought
Budapest, Aug 3: Hungary is entering its "most critical 5 days" as dropping water levels on the Danube River threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant amid an extreme heatwave, Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar has said, warning that the plant could be shut down for more than a month.
Speaking to local commercial television channel RTL on Sunday (local time), Magyar said the last remaining operating turbine at the 2,000 MW facility will likely be shut down late Sunday or on Monday. A complete halt to power generation at Paks, which accounts for nearly half of Hungary's domestic electricity generation, would mark the first full closure in the plant's 44-year history.
Magyar explained earlier on social media that strict nuclear safety regulations mandate the shutdown because of record-low river levels needed for cooling water, reports Xinhua news agency.
He reassured the public that nuclear safety remains fully guaranteed, with around 50 water management experts assisting plant personnel to maintain cooling operations.
The unprecedented energy crisis comes as Hungary braces for temperatures reaching 40 degrees Celsius or higher over these "most critical five days," placing immense strain on the national grid.
The Hungarian government has introduced emergency measures to maintain grid stability. Under a decree that took effect on Saturday, mandatory consumption cutbacks can be enforced on major industrial consumers if necessary.
However, Magyar noted that voluntary conservation efforts by businesses and the public have so far helped avoid enforced rationing. Major companies, including MOL, Audi, and Gedeon Richter, have pledged significant demand reductions.
Nearly 300 companies have already pledged voluntary reductions for Monday, along with numerous state-owned firms, most local councils, civil society groups and churches, he said.
To save power, decorative lighting on Budapest's iconic landmarks, including the Hungarian Parliament, Buda Castle, and the Chain Bridge, was turned off on Sunday evening.
Additional measures include halting most rail freight transport between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. starting Monday, bringing reserve power units on standby, and maximising electricity imports.
"If Hungary can get through these most critical five days, temperatures are expected to drop by 5 to 7 degrees Celsius," Magyar said, adding that household restrictions remain an absolute last resort to maintain system stability.
--IANS
